strengths: Novel and timely motivation: While visual prompt tuning (VPT) has become a prominent parameter-efficient adaptation paradigm, prompt tokens are typically opaque continuous vectors. Bridging VPT with concept prototype learning to make prompts semantically grounded and interpretable is a well-motivated and relatively unexplored direction.

Well-structured framework: The hierarchical design—comprising Concept Region Discovery (CRD), Intra-region Feature Aggregation (IFA), and fine-to-coarse prompt fusion across layers—provides an intuitive multi-granularity explanation mechanism.

Comprehensive quantitative interpretability benchmarking: The authors evaluate not only standard classification accuracy across five distinct backbones (DeiT-S/B and DinoV2-S/B/L) on CUB-200-2011, but also rigorous interpretability metrics (consistency and stability scores from Huang et al., 2023), demonstrating noticeable improvements over both classical prototype architectures and standard VPT baselines.
Clear qualitative evidence: The paper provides informative visualizations illustrating concept localization across bird species, histopathology (Gleason-2019), and vehicle parts (Stanford Cars).
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation on secondary datasets: Although the authors showcase qualitative examples on Gleason-2019 and Stanford Cars (Figures 7 and 8), quantitative results (such as classification accuracy or part-level metrics) are missing for these datasets in the main text, limiting the quantitative evaluation primarily to CUB-200-2011.

Missing efficiency and complexity analysis: One of the primary advantages of visual prompt tuning is parameter efficiency and low inference overhead. In IVPT, prompts are dynamically generated via spatial attention maps, distance calculations, and region aggregation at each layer. The manuscript lacks a discussion or empirical measurement of the parameter count, GPU memory footprint, and inference/training latency compared to standard VPT baselines.

Dependence and sensitivity to auxiliary losses: The unsupervised region discovery relies heavily on the part-shaping loss terms adapted from Pdiscoformer [1] alongside the consistency loss. The paper simply assigns equal weights of 1 to all terms without providing an ablation or sensitivity study regarding hyperparameter tuning for these loss components.

Clarity on the inference pipeline: Because prompts are derived from image patch embeddings via CRD and IFA, the exact execution order during feed-forward inference (e.g., whether patch embeddings from layer $i$ are used to generate prompt tokens for layer $i+1$ in a layer-by-layer dependency) should be described with greater operational clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: visual prompt tuning (VPT) is widely used for parameter-efficient adaptation, yet the learned prompt embeddings are opaque and lack human interpretability.

The proposed framework is conceptually sound and well-motivated. Grounding visual prompts in concept prototypes via Concept Region Discovery (CRD) and Intra-region Feature Aggregation (IFA), combined with fine-to-coarse hierarchical fusion across Transformer layers, offers an intuitive and structured way to interpret prompts.

The experimental evaluation on CUB-200-2011 is thorough across multiple model architectures (DeiT-S/B and DinoV2-S/B/L), measuring not only accuracy but also established interpretability metrics (consistency and stability scores).

Qualitative analyses across multiple domains—including fine-grained classification (CUB, Stanford Cars) and digital pathology (Gleason-2019)—effectively showcase the localized semantic regions captured by the learned concept prototypes.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation is largely restricted to a single benchmark (CUB-200-2011). While qualitative results are shown for Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019, reporting quantitative classification accuracy (and interpretability metrics where feasible) on these additional datasets would substantially reinforce the generalizability of the findings.

A key motivation for visual prompt tuning is efficiency. IVPT introduces patch-prototype distance computations, Gumbel-Softmax grouping, intra-region feature aggregation, and multiple auxiliary losses. The paper lacks an analysis of the computational overhead (training time, memory footprint, inference throughput, and trainable parameter count) compared to standard VPT.

Because the prompts in IVPT are generated by aggregating image patch embeddings within discovered concept regions (Equation 10), they appear to be input-dependent/dynamic prompts rather than static learned prefix tokens. The implications of this formulation on model architecture, inference latency, and conceptual comparison to standard static VPT should be clarified and explicitly discussed.

The paper lacks sensitivity analysis and ablations regarding key architectural hyperparameters, such as the layer-wise schedule of prototype numbers (17, 14, 11, 8), the number of fused prompts (4), and the weighting of the auxiliary losses.

strengths: Relevant and under-explored problem: Bringing interpretability to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) is an important and timely direction, addressing the black-box nature of learned continuous prompt tokens.

Well-structured framework: The hierarchical design that bridges fine-grained prompt prototypes in shallow layers to coarse-grained concepts in deeper layers via Gumbel-Softmax grouping and region consistency loss is intuitive and conceptually sound.

Comprehensive baselines on CUB-200-2011: The authors benchmark against both classical interpretable prototype models (ProtoPNet, ProtoPool, TesNet, Huang et al.) and modern VPT variants across multiple vision backbones (DeiT and DinoV2 families), demonstrating competitive consistency, stability, and classification accuracy.
weaknesses: Narrow quantitative evaluation: Quantitative evaluation (accuracy, consistency, and stability) is restricted solely to the CUB-200-2011 benchmark. While qualitative visualizations are shown for Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019, quantitative results (e.g., classification accuracy, part localization/IoU, or Gleason grading metrics) are missing. Furthermore, standard VPT benchmarks (such as VTAB-1k) are not evaluated.

Lack of efficiency and parameter analysis: A primary motivation of visual prompt tuning is parameter and computational efficiency. IVPT introduces multi-layer prototypes, spatial bias maps, grouping modules, intra-region feature aggregation, and multiple auxiliary losses, yet the manuscript provides no report on trainable parameter count, training overhead, memory footprint, or inference latency compared to standard VPT baselines.

Unclear semantic concept labeling process: In Figures 4, 7, and 8, concept prototypes are given specific semantic labels (e.g., 'Emblem/Handle', 'Rearview Mirrors', 'Glandular Lumen'). It is not clearly explained whether and how these text labels are assigned automatically or via post-hoc manual inspection, which slightly undermines the unsupervised claim.

Heavy reliance on existing loss formulations with limited self-contained details: The region discovery relies entirely on the part-shaping loss formulation from Pdiscoformer (Aniraj et al., 2024), but the exact formulation and weighting of these component losses within the IVPT pipeline are not sufficiently detailed in the main text.

Ambiguities in prompt propagation: Section 3 is somewhat ambiguous regarding how the fused prompts $P^{fs}$ interact with the backbone across successive layers. Clarification on the exact data flow between layer $i$ and layer $i+1$ (whether fused prompts replace input prompts in the next layer, or if intermediate prompts are passed directly) would improve technical reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) is typically treated as a black-box parameter-efficient adaptation technique. Bridging prompt tuning with concept-based interpretability and region grounding is an innovative and practically meaningful direction.

Intuitive cross-layer hierarchical design: Structuring concept prototypes across network layers—from fine-grained part semantics at lower layers to coarse-grained abstractions at deeper layers—paired with a grouping mechanism and cross-layer consistency loss ($L_{con}$), provides a coherent mechanism for hierarchical reasoning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is benchmarked across multiple ViT backbones (DeiT-S/B and DinoV2-S/B/L) and datasets (CUB-200-2011, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part), demonstrating solid quantitative improvements in interpretability metrics (Consistency and Stability) alongside competitive or improved classification accuracy.

Thorough appendix and ablation analyses: The submission provides helpful supplementary studies, including component ablations, layer-depth analysis, IoU consistency across layers, computational overhead breakdown, and human evaluation studies.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on existing part-discovery objectives: The region discovery and part regularization framework relies directly on the suite of part-shaping losses from Pdiscoformer (Aniraj et al., 2024) (including orthogonality, equivariance, presence, entropy, and total variation). While the adaptation into prompt generation and cross-layer fusion is novel, the core spatial grounding mechanism is largely borrowed.

Training overhead and equivariance computation: The equivariance loss ($L_{eq}$) requires applying random affine transformations and re-processing images through the backbone. Given that VPT aims for lightweight adaptation, the computational cost and memory footprint during training deserve clearer profiling in the main paper (e.g., peak GPU memory during the dual-pass training).

Clarity on baseline prompt implementations: In Table 1, several prompt tuning methods are augmented with prototype learning (e.g., 'VPT-Deep (w/ Proto.)'). The exact architecture and loss formulation for these hybrid baselines are only briefly described in the text; further elaboration is needed to clarify how much advantage stems from the cross-layer prompt fusion versus adding prototypes to the final layer.

Visual resolution and legibility: Figures 3, 8, 12, and 13 contain miniature visualization patches that are difficult to inspect without extreme magnification. Enhancing the zoom-in crops of representative part activations would strengthen the qualitative narrative.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored challenge in parameter-efficient fine-tuning: the lack of transparency and interpretability in visual prompt tuning (VPT).

The proposed method thoughtfully integrates concept discovery, spatial attribution, and prompt generation by grounding prompts in semantic image regions and hierarchically fusing fine-to-coarse concepts across transformer layers.
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple backbones (DeiT-S/B, DinoV2-S/B/L) and datasets (CUB-200-2011, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part, Gleason-2019, Stanford Cars, FGVC-Aircraft).
Extensive quantitative interpretability analysis using established consistency and stability metrics, accompanied by thorough ablation studies, cross-layer IoU analysis, and human evaluation studies.
weaknesses: Ambiguity regarding the frozen status of the backbone: While the main text emphasizes parameter-efficient visual prompt tuning with a frozen backbone (Section 3.1), Appendix A states that the class token, position embeddings, register tokens, and distillation tokens are fine-tuned. It is unclear whether all competing VPT baselines received the same tuning privileges.

Unclear metric implementation for baseline VPT: Standard visual prompt tuning methods (e.g., VPT-Shallow, VPT-Deep) output abstract embedding tokens without explicit spatial grounding or prototype correspondence. The paper does not adequately explain how the consistency and stability metrics (Huang et al., 2023) were computed for these vanilla VPT baselines in Table 1.

Increased architectural and objective complexity: Compared to standard lightweight VPT, IVPT introduces multiple extra components (spatial bias maps, prototype dictionaries across layers, grouping MLPs) and an extensive suite of part-shaping regularizers (orthogonality, equivariance, presence, entropy, total variation, and KL consistency). This introduces numerous hyperparameters and reduces the simplicity of prompt tuning.
Incomplete presentation details: The code repository link on page 1 is left blank ('Our code is available at').

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) typically learns abstract, continuous embeddings that lack semantic interpretability. Bridging parameter-efficient adaptation with concept-level prototype interpretability is a promising and timely research direction.

Methodological formulation: The paper designs a multi-stage mechanism comprising Concept Region Discovery (CRD) and Intra-region Feature Aggregation (IFA), along with a hierarchical cross-layer fusion scheme to capture fine-to-coarse semantics.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The authors conduct quantitative evaluations across multiple backbones (DeiT-S/B, DinoV2-S/B/L) and datasets (CUB-200-2011, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part) using established interpretability metrics (Consistency and Stability) as well as classification accuracy.

Comprehensive qualitative and user studies: The manuscript includes numerous visualizations (fine-grained birds, cars, aircraft, pathology whole-slide patches), failure analyses, ablation studies, and a 20-participant human evaluation study.
weaknesses: Deviation from standard Parameter-Efficient Prompt Tuning protocol: According to Appendix A, the class token, position embeddings, register tokens (in DinoV2), and distillation tokens (in DeiT) are all unfrozen and trained alongside prototypes and bias maps. In standard Visual Prompt Tuning (e.g., Jia et al., 2022), the backbone (including positional embeddings and class tokens) is completely frozen while only prefix prompt embeddings are learned. Unfreezing positional embeddings and tokens provides significant adaptation capacity, making the performance comparison against purely frozen-backbone VPT baselines potentially unfair.

Blurry distinction between VPT and Part-Prototype Discovery Networks: The proposed prompts are not learnable input prefix tokens that guide frozen attention layers; rather, they are dynamically generated feature aggregations from image patch representations conditioned on prototype attention maps (Eq. 1–3, 7). Furthermore, classification is performed using dedicated heads on the final layer's concept prompts (Eq. 4). This architecture functions more like a part-prototype discovery network (closely following PDiscoFormer and ProtoPNet) than visual prompt tuning.

Heavy reliance on existing loss formulations with limited sensitivity analysis: The core mechanism that enables localized, non-overlapping part discovery relies on five distinct part-shaping loss terms directly taken from PDiscoFormer (Aniraj et al., 2024; Appendix B). While the paper sets lambda weights to 1, there is minimal analysis or ablation showing how sensitive the framework is to the weighting of these multiple regularization terms.

Writing and presentation polish: The abstract ends with an incomplete sentence ('Our code is available at '), and several citations are rendered with raw LaTeX symbols (e.g., 'E^2vpt' on page 12). Additionally, the exact dataflow of how fused prompts Pf_s interact with intermediate Transformer layers versus the patch tokens would benefit from clearer mathematical notation in Section 3.3.
